cases.abstract: Conformal risk control extends prediction-set calibration from binary coverage errors to graded losses. It selects a parameter by thresholding an average of n calibration losses and the upper bound B for an unseen loss. For exchangeable, right-continuous losses bounded above by B, nonincreasing in the parameter and with an endpoint loss at most alpha, the selected parameter guarantees expected test loss at most alpha. Under stronger assumptions of independent, identically distributed nonnegative losses and zero probability of a jump at any fixed parameter, expected loss is also at least alpha - 2B/(n + 1). Examples show that this general lower bound cannot be tightened, limiting how conservative the calibration can be in that setting. Segmentation, multilabel and hierarchical classification, and question answering illustrate nonbinary risk control across 1,000 random splits. The guarantee averages over calibration and test data rather than holding for each fitted set. Without monotonicity, expected loss can approach B despite a lower target; a monotone upper envelope restores control but can sacrifice informativeness when the original loss is far from monotone.
cases.methods: Simply thresholding mean calibration loss leaves the unseen test loss unaccounted for. Conformal risk control instead defines R_n(lambda) as the mean of n calibration losses bounded above by B and selects the smallest parameter satisfying [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n + 1) <= alpha. If no parameter qualifies, it uses an endpoint whose loss is at most alpha. The correction upper-bounds the average that would include the test observation. An oracle using all n + 1 losses would therefore select a parameter no larger than the implementable choice. Conditional on their unordered collection, exchangeability makes the oracle's expected test loss equal their average; right-continuity ensures that average meets the target. Since the losses are nonincreasing, the implementable parameter cannot increase loss relative to the oracle. The empirical rule thus inherits a finite-sample expectation guarantee rather than relying on calibrated model probabilities.
cases.results: The correction produced mean risks close to the target in two nonbinary false-negative applications, rather than substantial undershooting. Across 1,000 random splits at alpha = 0.1, polyp segmentation yielded mean risk 0.0987 and standard deviation 0.0114, using 1,000 calibration and 781 evaluation images. MS COCO multilabel classification yielded 0.0996 and 0.0052, respectively, with 4,000 calibration and 1,000 evaluation images under the same target and split count. Segmentation varied more across splits, but its different task and calibration size prevent isolating why. That variation does not contradict expected-risk control: the guarantee averages over calibration and test data, rather than constraining every split or image. The nonmonotone counterexample supplies the complementary boundary. Without monotonicity, the unmodified rule can attain expected loss arbitrarily near B despite a lower target. The applications therefore support near-target calibration for the tested monotone losses, while the counterexample explains why monotonicity remains a consequential condition.
cases.notes: Revision retains the original theorem-centered allocation. The abstract's correction-to-guarantee link and the Methods oracle comparison use Theorem 1; the tightness claim uses Theorem 2 and Proposition 1. Results compare proximity to alpha and split dispersion in Sections 3.1-3.2, not accuracy or independent training trials. The nonmonotone boundary uses Proposition 2. Reporting queries remain about the multilabel false-positive wording, QA threshold orientation, and shift monotonicity; none is needed to support the selected claims.

cases.abstract: Distribution shifts can invalidate a fixed conformal calibration level even when models and score quantiles are updated. Adaptive conformal inference uses each revealed coverage error to adjust the quantile level: a miss moves calibration toward larger sets, whereas a covered response moves it toward smaller ones. With quantile extensions permitting full or empty sets, the feedback recursion bounds cumulative miscoverage error and guarantees convergence of the long-run empirical miscoverage frequency to the target without distributional assumptions. This controls accumulated errors, not coverage at every time point. Stronger concentration and approximate marginal-coverage bounds are established in a hidden Markov setting with fixed fitted functions, stationary initialization and additional regularity conditions. Volatility forecasts and county-vote predictions ordered by time zone show smaller local coverage departures than fixed-level calibration in the reported comparisons. Unnormalized volatility scores nevertheless produce wider swings even with adaptation, so feedback does not remove dependence on score design. The step size balances responsiveness against instability, and the online procedure assumes each response is available for the next update.
cases.methods: At time t, prediction sets include responses whose scores are at or below the 1 - alpha_t quantile. Once the response is revealed, adaptive conformal inference updates alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha - err_t), where alpha is the target miscoverage, gamma is positive and err_t indicates a miss. A miss lowers the level, relaxing the inclusion cutoff; a covered response reverses this adjustment. Summing the recursion shows that average miscoverage differs from alpha by (alpha_1 - alpha_{T+1})/(gamma T). Extending quantiles outside [0, 1] to produce full or empty sets keeps alpha_t between -gamma and 1 + gamma. Thus bounded parameter motion, rather than a correct model of the shifting distribution, makes the average discrepancy vanish as T grows. This operation controls accumulated coverage error, but its guarantee permits extreme sets and does not ensure accurate coverage in short windows.
cases.results: At step size 0.005, adaptive calibration with normalized volatility scores tracked the 90% coverage target more closely than fixed calibration in the displayed failure cases. Both methods used rolling 1,250-day histories for GARCH forecasts and score quantiles. The adaptive 500-day local coverage curves stayed within the fluctuations illustrated by an i.i.d. Bernoulli comparator, whereas fixed calibration undercovered Fannie Mae during the 2008 crisis. The four panels were selected from twelve stocks because the fixed method failed visibly, so they illustrate specific failures. Replacing normalized scores with unnormalized absolute errors produced wider swings even under adaptation; feedback alone therefore did not stabilize local coverage in that configuration. For county-vote predictions ordered by time zone and randomized within zones, adaptive calibration maintained approximately 90% coverage in 300-county windows, while fixed calibration developed troughs at zone changes. This comparison supports adaptation under constructed reporting drift rather than an actual election-night replay.
cases.notes: The abstract's convergence claim and Methods explanation use Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.1. Results test local coverage using Figures 1-3: normalized-score adaptation versus fixed calibration, the adverse score contrast, and constructed time-zone drift. Bernoulli curves remain descriptive comparators. Stock plots use centered 500-day windows, not trailing windows; the selected four stocks are failure examples among twelve. The stronger theory in Section 4.2 assumes fixed fitted functions and stationary initialization, unlike rolling refitting in the applications. The county experiment does not replay actual reporting order.
